title: Java Classes/Objects
learningObjectives: Declare a Java class with fields and methods.
Create an object using the new keyword.
Access public members through an object reference.
Explain that separate instances have independent instance fields.
Use dot notation to call an object's method or read an accessible member.

understand.concept: A class declares members such as fields, constructors and methods. The new keyword creates an object and returns a reference to it. A variable of a class type stores that reference, and dot notation accesses members allowed by Java's access rules.
understand.whyItMatters: Classes and objects provide the basic building blocks for modelling entities such as students, products and accounts. Multiple objects can share one class definition but maintain separate instance state.
understand.analogy: Think of a well-designed object as a small service with a clear responsibility: it keeps the information it owns and exposes only the operations other code needs.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy is only a design aid; Java access, inheritance and dispatch follow the language's exact rules.

explain.narrative:
## Declare a class

Write a class with a name and braces. Fields represent object state and methods define behaviour. A class can be declared in the same source file as Main when it is not public.

## Create and use objects

Use `new ClassName()` to create an instance. Store the returned reference in a variable and use dot notation to access accessible fields and methods.

## Instance identity

Each call to `new` creates a distinct object. Assigning one reference variable to another copies the reference, not the object itself.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting `new` when creating an object.
- Trying to access an inaccessible private member directly.
- Assuming two object variables always refer to two separate objects.

examples.title: Declare a class and object
examples.code:
class Car { String model = "Civic"; }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Car car = new Car(); System.out.println(car.model); } }
examples.explanation: new Car() creates an instance and car refers to it.

examples.title: Call an object method
examples.code:
class Speaker { void sayHello() { System.out.println("Hello"); } }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Speaker speaker = new Speaker(); speaker.sayHello(); } }
examples.explanation: Dot notation calls a method on the referenced object.

examples.title: Create independent instances
examples.code:
class Box { int size; }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Box small = new Box(); Box large = new Box(); small.size = 2; large.size = 9; System.out.println(small.size + ":" + large.size); } }
examples.explanation: Each instance has its own size field.

examples.title: Two variables can share one reference
examples.code:
class Note { String text; }
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { Note first = new Note(); Note second = first; second.text = "Shared"; System.out.println(first.text); } }
examples.explanation: Both variables refer to the same object.

examples.title: Pass an object to a method
examples.code:
class Badge { String label = "Guest"; }
public class Main { static void print(Badge badge) { System.out.println(badge.label); } public static void main(String[] args) { print(new Badge()); } }
examples.explanation: A method parameter can receive an object reference value.

questions.prompt: Which keyword creates a new object?
questions.explanation: The new expression constructs an object.

questions.prompt: How do you call an accessible method on an object named user?
questions.explanation: Java uses dot notation followed by parentheses for a method call.

questions.prompt: What happens when two variables are assigned the same object reference?
questions.answer: Both variables refer to the same object
options: Both variables refer to the same object
A deep copy is always created
questions.explanation: Reference assignment copies the reference value.

questions.prompt: What does an instance field represent?
questions.answer: State belonging to an individual object
options: State belonging to an individual object
A value shared by all classes
questions.explanation: Each object has its own instance fields.

questions.prompt: Which declaration creates an object of class Book?
questions.explanation: The new expression constructs the Book instance.
